newsitem.title: USA: Cigarettes on the way out, so look on the lighter side for assets.
newsitem.headline: Cigarettes on the way out, so look on the lighter side for assets.

text.p: Cigarettes are on the way out, so it's time to look on the lighter side if you're looking for a hot asset.

Those little flame-makers -- whose shapes range from Zippo's familiar flattened cylinder to pistols, walking sticks, cameras or fanciful hand carvings -- are now prized valuables sometimes worth thousands of dollars.
"It's an art form that's almost lost. It's utilitarian. They were representations of class and style," said Karen Cairo who with her husband, Terry, own 6,000 lighters.
"There's historical significance. Guys in trenches made lighters when didn't have anything else to do. Almost everybody's father, mother or grandfather used a lighter. It brings back fond memories."
Collectors began to stock up on lighters about 10 years ago, as smoking started to wane and an abundance of interesting specimens that cost next to nothing showed up at garage sales and flea markets.
Their popularity and prices have steadily risen as the Japanese passion for Americana burgeoned and Americans started to value lighters as a kind of relic, like typewriters and fountain pens.
Recently, a resurgence in cigar smoking has fuelled demand for fancy lighters to match the fancy habit.

"Five years ago you could pick up gas Dunhills for under $50. Now Dunhills retail for $400," Cairo said. "The secondary market has since cropped up especially since cigar smokers prefer to use gas Dunhills."

In the heirarchy of lighters, pre-1950s models fuelled by lighter fluid have the greatest cachet, especially if made by such names as Cartier, Dunhill, Ronson, Faberge or Tiffany. "Touch-tip" lighters with a metal wand, made until the 1940s, fetch a premium. The wand has a wick at one end that sits in a small reservoir of chemicals. It lights up when you push a plunger that spins the spark wheel.

Lighters made after 1950 burn butane at the flick of a wheel and possess as much aura as disposable ball point pens -- unless of course, they carry images that thrill collectors of Americana or celebrity memorabilia.

Among the most expensive lighters is a solid 18-carat gold Cartier from 1909 shaped like a Browning pistol. The only one known to exist, the pocket lighter is valued at $25,000 by its owner Ira Pilossof, who has a dealership, Vintage Lighters Inc., in Fair Lawn, N.J. (1-888-4-LIGHTER)
Terry Cairo was recently offered $15,000 for an unusually plain Faberge lighter from the turn of century that he had bought six months earlier for $1,200. He turned it down.
A late 1920s Dunhill walking stick whose top opens up to reveal a lighter is worth at least $10,000 to $15,000.

An even more ingenious lighter is contained in a miniature bar with a black bartender. The wand handle sticks out from the countertop. The sides of the bar open to reveal cigarettes. This mid-1930s object d'art by Ronson costs $1,800, compared with $800 about 10 years ago.
But plenty of lower-priced lighters, from $10 to $15, are available for collectors with a smaller budget. In any case, it's still a good time to buy at the high end.
"Prices haven't peaked. It's still a fairly new (hobby). People stopping smoking has only helped it, and there's big Japanese interest in Zippos," Pilossof said.

Zippo's first lighter from 1932 is now worth $5,000. It looks much like the chrome-plated brass lighters still made by the Bradford, Pa.-based company, which is setting up a new museum and holds a convention for collectors every July.
Zippos from 1932 through the 1960s are the most popular, largely among foreign collectors of Americana looking for images of early advertising and icons like Mickey Mouse.
"A plain Zippo from the 1950s costs only $10. But if you put the Empire State Building on it, it's $50," Pilossof said.
Novelty also counts. Lighters that sit atop models of the old Pan Am building in New York, the Seattle Space Needle or other landmarks attract more buyers.
Lighters marked "Made in Occupied Japan" or "Made in U.S. Zone -- Germany" -- made after World War II -- are hot items, no matter what the brand is.

"Trench" lighters made by soldiers during the two World Wars -- because matches got wet in the trenches -- are also highly sought after. These were made of spare metal parts or coins and cotton, and were fuelled by kerosene or gasoline.
Surprisingly, chrome lighters are worth far more than silver ones, which were made in abundance in Mexico, India and Pakistan, Cairo said.

Several books on lighters and price guides have been published in recent years. These include "Collectors Guide to Cigarette Lighters" by James Flanagan, published by Collector Books of Paduka, Ky.; and "Cigarette Lighters" by Stewart Schneider & Fischler, published by Schiffer. Clubs include the Pocket Lighter Preservation Guild and Historical Society and On the Lighter Side, International Lighter Collectors.
